text: The trouble was getting there.
Land six miles out is worthless if no one can reach it, and in the early 1850s there was no easy way down.
A person could ride out by carriage over rough ground, but no one was going to do that twice a day to get to work.
So Cornell made the deal that built the neighborhood.
The Illinois Central Railroad was laying its line south along the lakefront in those years, and Cornell saw exactly what it could do for him.
He handed the railroad sixty acres of his ground for the right of way.
In return he got a station at 53rd Street and a commitment to commuter trains running into the city, a daily service into the Great Central Depot downtown.
The first passenger runs came in 1856, and a trip that had once taken the better part of an afternoon now took about twenty minutes.
That single bargain is the hinge of the whole story.
Cornell gave away a fifth of his land to make the other four-fifths reachable, and the moment it was reachable, prairie started turning into suburb.
Distance was the only thing he was really selling, and the train is what turned distance from a liability into a luxury.
You could live by the lake and still be at your desk downtown before the morning was out.
The railroad handed him a new problem, though.
A station needs passengers, and there was almost nothing out there yet to draw them.
At one point the railroad even threatened to stop the service for lack of riders.
So Cornell built the draw himself.
In 1857 he put up the Hyde Park House, a four-story wood-frame hotel set right by the water near the 53rd Street tracks.
It was a resort, plainly.
It had a ballroom and a dining room and views straight out over Lake Michigan, and Cornell said later that the cost of it almost broke him.
He was not building a hotel so much as building a reason to come.
Wealthy Chicagoans rode the train down on summer weekends, looked at the lake, ate well, and some of them looked at the empty lots and started to imagine a house there.
